newsitem.title: BOSNIA: U.S. to fund Bosnia railway repairs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to fund Bosnia railway repairs.

text.p: The United States plans to spend more than $5 million to reconstruct Bosnia's war-damaged nothern railway linking the country to the rest of Europe, a U.S. official said on Wednesday.
Bosnia's T-shaped railway system, running east-west and north-south, was heavily damaged during the 1992-1995 war.

The U.S. Agency for International Development will fund railway repairs inside Bosnia and neighbouring Croatia to make the railway network operational by September, U.S. presidential envoy Claude Ganz told reporters.
The project will require the laying of 14 km (eight miles) of new track, the construction of two bridges and the completion of a bridge spanning the Sava river on the Bosnia-Croatia border.
A U.S. firm, Ralph M. Parsons company, is overseeing the railway project, with local Bosnian or Croatian firms bidding to provide labour, Western officials said.
Parsons won a contract last year worth about $10 million to manage U.S.-funded reconstruction projects in former Yugoslavia.
Ganz said repairing the railway does not mean trains will start running immediately to Budapest, because rival Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders have yet to agree on the use of the network.
"We have found a way to make Bosnian trains connect to Europe, now it's up to the political leadership to make it happen," he said.
The Bosnian railway's east-west link and a southwest line were repaired last year through international funding and assistance from NATO engineers.
But the lines are not being used due to political disputes over how to organise rail transport to Croatia and across Bosnia's Serb and Moslem-Croat entities.

Bosnia will have to come to an agreement with neighbouring Croatia on opening borders to trade. The country's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic also need to agree on the free passage of trains, Ganz said.

Political haggling between Bosnia and Croatia and inside Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation has stifled rail traffic between Sarajevo and the Adriatic coast, a year after the much-celebrated reopening of the Sarajevo-Ploce link.
Despite political difficulties surrounding the revival of the railways, Ganz said he was optimistic and predicted the northern line would not be idle.
"Our confidence is in the Bosnian government leadership to make this happen. There are absolutely no reasons why it shouldn't and there is no logical reason why they shouldn't do it," he said.
Asked if politicians had offered pledges that they would start running trains on the northern railway, Ganz said: "We have no commitments, no".
